title: US forest-bird counts after 2024 hurricane winds of 83 kt or more agreed with the published 9% decrease, but 16 routes did not exclude zero; satellite canopy loss did not explain the decrease
abstract: Question: does the published result that forest-bird counts on North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes fall about 9% after modelled hurricane winds of 83 kt or more (sci:78f2, storms 1981-2023) repeat for the 2024 storms, and does measured canopy loss explain it? Approach: we ran the published 78f2 code with the 2026 BBS release (surveys to 2025) and IBTrACS to 2025, with a pre-registered plan. We added route NDVI from PKU GIMMS v1.2 (1982-2022) as a damage measure, and stop noise and car counts as detection checks. Results: the refit gave the published -9.4% (95% CI -15.1 to -3.6). Under the published design only 1 route had 83 kt or more in 2024, because Florida routes had earlier storms (Ian, Idalia), so the registered test was not possible. With no prior-season filter (not registered), 16 routes (Helene, Milton) gave -8.8% (-18.9 to +1.3): close to the prediction, but the interval includes zero (detectable effect about 15%). Winds of 83 kt or more decreased autumn NDVI by 0.015 (-0.027 to -0.003), but next-summer NDVI changed little. The pre-registered damage interaction for forest birds was +4.4% per SD of NDVI loss (+1.1 to +7.6), but it had a pre-storm term of +2.2% and was not clear with a pre-mean reference (+2.9%, -0.6 to +6.4) or with more storms (+2.1%, -1.6 to +5.8). Damage explained about 11% of the 83 kt decrease. Open-habitat birds also decreased (-7.5%). Woodpeckers decreased most (-21%, -33 to -10, for three years; exploratory). Stop noise did not clearly increase. Limitations: small new sample, modelled wind, coarse 8 km NDVI, counts mix abundance and detection.

Only the pre-registered k = -1 model gave a clear forest-bird term, and its pre-storm placebo had the same sign.
